newsitem.title: USA: COLUMN - Post-election blues for Clinton, Gingrich?.
newsitem.headline: COLUMN - Post-election blues for Clinton, Gingrich?.

text.p: (The following is an opinion column by Allan J. Lichtman, a political historian with the American University in Washington DC. This views expressed are those of the author and do not reflect Reuters)
By Allan J. Lichtman
President Clinton and House Speaker Newt Gingrich may soon find themselves saying with the Duke of Wellington that "nothing except a battle lost can be half so melancholy as a battle won."
Both look like winning re-election in November, but both may face rocky times thereafter when scandals and legal problems, delayed by the campaign, come home to haunt them.
Shortly after the election, the Supreme Court will decide whether Paula Jones' sexual harassment suit can be heard while Clinton serves as president.

Meanwhile, Special Prosecutor Kenneth Starr is relentlessly investigating the Clintons' involvement in Whitewater, the firing of White House travel office employees and the receipt of confidential FBI files on former White House employees.
Starr may be competent and fair-minded, but he's a partisan Republican who will dig for incriminating evidence against the Clintons and make the most of what he finds.

How many government officials in this era of borderline business deals and complicated regulations would survive a dedicated prosecutor with $50 million to plumb the depths of their public and private lives?

The investigation against Gingrich is less intense but may be even more dangerous. The Georgia lawmaker will face grave charges that he violated tax laws in financing his college course on "Renewing American Civilisation."
My prediction is that Gingrich will not last another year as speaker even if the Republicans retain control of the House in November.
Charges against Gingrich have been pending for two years in the bipartisan House ethics committee. Last December, the Committee appointed James Cole as outside counsel to investigate the allegations.
Cole recently filed a report summarizing the evidence in the Gingrich case, but House Republicans blocked its release. Allegedly, the report contains information highly damaging to the speaker.
The Cole report will probably stay buried until after Election Day. But charges against the speaker will be heard next year.

Gingrich may be hoist on his own petard. In 1989, when the House probed ethics charges against Speaker James Wright, Gingrich pushed the investigation to a speedy conclusion and insisted that a speaker must be above even the appearance of wrongdoing.
Beyond his legal problems, Clinton faces an extraordinary historical challenge. Every two-term Democratic president of the last 100 years has faced a grim second-term slump.
The Great Depression of the 1890s ravaged America during Grover Cleveland's second term.
Woodrow Wilson won victories in World War I but botched the peace.
Franklin Roosevelt launched ill-fated schemes to pack the Supreme Court and purge conservatives from the Democratic Party.
Harry Truman lost China to the Communists, fell short of victory in Korea and failed enact his Fair Deal proposals.
Lyndon Johnson fell victim to his disastrous escalation in Vietnam.

Roosevelt ran for a third term in 1940 and won, but Republicans succeeded each of the other four two-term Democrats. Not since Martin Van Buren succeeded Andrew Jackson in 1840 has a two-term Democratic president turned the White House over to a successor of his own party.
Clinton's political skill may help him break the two-term Democratic jinx. But history also teaches that scandals usually erupt during a president's second term.
Examples include Watergate, Iran/Contra, and the Truman-era corruption that became known as the "mess in Washington."

Clinton and Gingrich, arguably the two most powerful politicians in the United States, appear to be in for the political battles of their lives -- battles that have nothing to do with the upcoming election.
